show_hn.title: Show HN: Lightscale AI – A language for LLMs to write business software
show_hn.story_text:
I am Luc, one of the co-founders of Lightscale AI. I have background in programming languages (ETH Zurich) and we are small team in Zug, Switzerland. As more and more code is now written by LLMs and few people have time to review the generated code, we came up with the idea to revise the actual stack below the LLMs: The programming language with its compiler and runtime system, all designed from scratch for AI authorship, not for humans. We have three goals:
1. Security and stability by language design: Some classes of errors are removed by abstraction as the AI never writes that code, but the compiler and runtime implement it fully. Others are reduced by  rigid compiler checks and very strict language rules (no fun for humans to code).

show_hn.title: Show HN: Evalkit for Improving Your Agents
show_hn.story_text: I wanted to share evalkit - an open source framework for improving agents that we built. https://evalkit.inferedge.com/ Like most people, we used phoenix, langfuse, but these are good recording traces, managing datasets etc. But the process around evals, agent improvements, regressions, mapping errors/failures to code or prompts has to be hand rolled. We still use self-hosted phoenix, but mainly as a database. Our process was trace mining, converting them into evals, getting them reviewed by an expert, and then re-running datasets to create baseline scores or internal benchmarks for our agents. We found other companies also follow similar processes in-house, but there is no good framework to do everything e2e.

Show HN: Fmgrep – indexed grep over a persistent FM index
show_hn.story_text: fmgrep is a (Claude-powered) open source reimplementation of a FAANG code search engine I was involved in a few years back. It's aimed at very large (e.g. AOSP) source trees. Back then we wanted to get our hands on the Github search engine (https://github.com/danlark1/sparse_ngrams) but it was not available, so we went a different way. Instead of n-grams,`fmgrep` builds an FM index of the tree with O(pattern) `count` and O(occurrences) `locate`, which is quite cool and leads to blazing fast performance as seen in the benchmarks.
